sections.heading: 1. Assign accountable seats before adding inboxes or clients
paragraphs: Start Candidate #18 with one full-time owner and three contractors, not four interchangeable outreach generalists. The owner holds sales, pricing, customer acceptance definitions, collections, and final account accountability. Contractor one owns account research, contact provenance, deduplication, and suppression matching. Contractor two owns authenticated sending infrastructure, sequence deployment, mailbox monitoring, and technical incident recovery. Contractor three owns reply triage, qualification evidence, appointment confirmation, and CRM disposition. Each responsibility needs a primary owner, a documented backup, and an observable completion artifact. In the four-person pod, backups provide limited continuity rather than another full production shift. Maintain Candidate #18's 54 mapped plays in one responsibility register, preserving their existing identifiers and assigning exactly one accountable seat per play. Add fields for required inputs, completion evidence, service deadline, exception owner, and recovery instructions. Do not invent fifty-four new initiatives or run every play simultaneously. Activate only the subset needed for the current offer and channel, while retaining ownership for dormant plays. A HubSpot pipeline, a Google Workspace evidence folder, and a password manager can support this structure without hiring a separate operations manager. Separate client workspaces and access permissions from the start.

Contractor statements of work should purchase defined outcomes and service availability rather than disguise employment through invoices. An illustrative Base monthly schedule pays research $1,800, delivery infrastructure $2,200, and qualification $1,500, totaling $5,500 monthly or $66,000 annually before separately budgeted incentives. These are planning assumptions, not required market rates or the entire expense base. Specify accepted account batches, monitored mailbox capacity, qualified reply coverage, and rework responsibility against each fee. Require research corrections within two business days, urgent suppression propagation within one business day, and reply routing within four covered business hours. Define coverage hours explicitly; a small pod cannot silently promise continuous service. Pay agreed base invoices on time and attach any variable reward to audited accepted outcomes, not sends or raw appointments. Investigate whether federal common-law employment factors and applicable state tests permit each arrangement; California Labor Code section 2775 can impose an ABC test subject to statutory exceptions. A contractor label does not settle classification. Preserve genuine control over work methods where appropriate, and use employment when the actual relationship requires it. The fee schedule must also identify which tools the business purchases directly and which contractor costs are included.

At Scaled, add one full-time client operations lead and one contractor dedicated to independent QA and routing audits. The owner retains commercial strategy and major renewals; the new employee owns routine customer reviews, capacity planning, collections follow-through, and incident coordination. Research, infrastructure, and qualification remain distinct contractor seats, while the fourth contractor samples their outputs without approving their own production. This produces exactly two full-time people plus four contractors, not a hidden seventh account manager. Hire against sustained workload and projected contribution, not a single unusually large order. For four consecutive weeks, record minutes spent on accepted outcomes, rework, customer meetings, and exceptions; reserve twenty percent of scheduled delivery capacity for variability. As an illustrative capacity test, eighteen clients requiring three weekly account-service hours consume fifty-four hours before prospecting production. That load cannot fit inside a single forty-hour seat and requires narrower service scope, redistributed work, or fewer clients. Maintain tested playbooks for domain loss, calendar failure, absent contractors, and disputed qualification. Each active mapped play should survive a planned five-business-day absence of its primary operator before further client volume is added. Measure continuity with completed artifacts, not assurances.

sections.heading: 2. Pay for accepted demand and run one weekly evidence review
paragraphs: Define the commercial acceptance event before calculating any KPI. For a qualified appointment, require the agreed company segment, geography, role or purchasing influence, relevant business need, and an explicit meeting commitment. State whether the purchased unit is a booked meeting, a held meeting, or a qualified connected call; these are different products and cannot share an ambiguous fee trigger. A call-routing agreement should specify minimum connection conditions, duplicate lookback, excluded callers, and evidence retained. Store timestamps and qualification fields in HubSpot or Salesforce, linking each event to campaign, customer, contractor, and source cohort. Record an appointment identifier that persists through rescheduling so one prospect does not become three billed outcomes. Give customers a defined evidence-based review period, such as five business days, with escalation for substantive disputes. Silence should count as acceptance only when the signed agreement expressly provides that mechanism. Keep rejected, credited, and disputed events visible rather than deleting them to improve conversion reports. For every rejection, distinguish targeting failure, false qualification, duplicate delivery, customer scheduling failure, and prospect withdrawal. Those causes drive different remedies and prevent contractors from absorbing losses they did not cause.

Run a thirty-minute weekly review using a frozen reporting window and a small set of reproducible ratios. Acceptance rate equals accepted submissions divided by submissions whose review period has closed; hold rate equals held meetings divided by meetings whose scheduled time has passed. Report unresolved submissions separately rather than counting them as successes. Add credited fees divided by originally billed outcome fees, median routing latency, reply coverage attainment, and customer-level contribution after direct labor and attributable tools. Inspect positive replies and qualified outcomes by domain and source cohort, while treating open rates as diagnostic noise rather than a payment basis. Initial internal targets might be at least eighty-five percent acceptance, seventy-five percent held meetings, no more than five percent credited outcome fees, and ninety-five percent routing within the contracted service window. These are explicit starting assumptions to recalibrate against segment economics, not universal industry benchmarks. Any suppression failure receives immediate investigation even when aggregate KPIs look healthy. Close the meeting with one named owner and one deadline for each exception. Avoid twenty competing dashboard tiles that leave nobody accountable for the customer experience.

Design incentives so good qualification pays more than calendar stuffing. An illustrative contractor bonus pays $15 for each incremental accepted held meeting above the agreed baseline, provided the sampled qualification audit meets its threshold and the contractor-controlled routing SLA is satisfied. Forty eligible meetings produce a $600 bonus; include that cost in the campaign's contribution calculation before offering the arrangement. Do not retroactively change earned compensation because a customer pays late; define any collection-dependent component prospectively in the agreement. Audit every customer dispute plus ten randomly selected submissions per active contractor weekly, or all submissions when volume is smaller. The owner performs this check in the starting pod; the independent QA contractor performs it at Scaled. Preserve the sample selection method to deter cherry-picking. Multi-inbox infrastructure must respect provider terms, accurate sender identity, applicable opt-out duties, and recipient preferences; extra domains are not permission to evade blocks. CAN-SPAM, 15 U.S.C. section 7704, applies to commercial email including B2B messages. Phone workflows require separate assessment under 47 U.S.C. section 227 and 47 CFR section 64.1200; a business label alone does not resolve technology, number-type, or consent requirements.

Subtract allocated delivery labor, incentives, and attributable tools from revenue

Compare opt-out timestamps against subsequent sends and routing eligibility

sop_steps.action: Export matured submissions, scheduled meetings, credits, routing events, and contractor coverage records.
sop_steps.detail: Use one timezone, persistent event identifiers, and a dated export so later edits cannot silently change the reviewed denominator.

sections.heading: 3. Reconcile accrual earnings and cap transferable-book concentration
paragraphs: Reconcile every operating plan to the canonical scenarios before discussing growth. Conservative revenue of $100,000 less $80,000 of expenses produces $20,000 owner net profit at twenty percent. Base revenue of $425,000 less $297,500 produces $127,500 at thirty percent. Scaled revenue of $750,000 less $450,000 produces $300,000 at forty percent. Those totals describe retainers and accepted-lead fees, excluding client-funded advertising pass-through; they do not describe customer pipeline value, merchant sales, or prospective deal size. An illustrative Base bridge uses five customers paying $5,000 monthly retainers, producing $300,000, plus 500 accepted outcomes billed at $250, producing $125,000. This assumes full-year retention and separate contractual deliverables for the retainer and outcome fee. Allocate one hundred accepted outcomes to each customer and annual revenue becomes $85,000 per customer, or twenty percent each. Monthly recognized revenue averages $35,416.67 but cash receipts can differ materially. The $66,000 illustrative contractor base fees belong inside the $297,500 Base expense envelope, leaving $231,500 for all remaining costs and adjustments. Do not treat that remainder as another profit pool. Document actual payroll, tools, acquisition, insurance, refunds, and overhead against it.

Close the books monthly on a consistent accrual basis, with customer contracts defining service periods and acceptance evidence supporting earned fees. Advance retainer cash becomes deferred revenue until the contracted service is delivered; an annual prepayment is not automatically current-month earnings. Accrue contractor work already performed even when an invoice arrives next month, and estimate credits using documented disputes and cohort experience. Use QuickBooks Online or Xero customer dimensions, supported by a CRM event ledger, to reconcile invoices, recognized revenue, credits, cash, and receivables. Track advertising funds in separate clearing records consistent with the contractual principal-agent arrangement; never inflate the canonical operator revenue with customer media spend. Build monthly acquisition cohorts showing first service date, opening recurring fees, expansion, contraction, churn, accepted outcomes, and direct delivery cost. Net revenue retention measures retained recurring fees plus expansion minus contraction and churn against the same opening customer cohort; disclose whether variable outcome fees are included. Report fixed-retainer retention separately when variable volumes obscure stability. Reconcile aged receivables to customer disputes, since apparently profitable delivery can consume cash when acceptance remains unresolved. A buyer should trace any reported cohort total back to individual events and signed scopes.

Set a maximum twenty-five percent exposure to any customer group, referral counterparty, or material delivery counterparty, measured against the relevant denominator. Combine affiliates under common control; five invoices to one corporate parent do not create diversification. For customers, measure trailing-twelve-month recognized revenue and forward ninety-day contracted revenue separately. For referral partners, measure the revenue of accounts they control or can withdraw. For nonexclusive delivery vendors, measure critical production capacity and document substitute availability. During startup, a single first customer necessarily breaches the customer cap; label that exposure openly and avoid claiming the transferable-book standard has been met. Stop expanding that account until diversification restores the limit, unless consciously accepting a documented temporary exception. Prefer twenty percent as the operating target so a neighboring account's churn does not immediately create a breach. Where a core CRM or mailbox provider cannot practically meet the counterparty limit, report the exception and test export, restoration, and alternate-provider migration. Splitting mailboxes into multiple tenants at the same provider does not diversify that dependency. Concentration is a transferable earnings issue: losing one account must not destroy the pod's ability to cover its fixed obligations.

callout.body: These four checks establish whether the pod's reported earnings can survive operational and buyer scrutiny.
items: Recalculate all three canonical revenue-minus-expense bridges and confirm that customer-funded advertising never enters the operator revenue numerator.
Verify that every active mapped play has an accountable seat, an authorized backup, measurable acceptance evidence, and a tested recovery instruction.

sections.heading: 4. Transfer enforceable assets and value the earnings a buyer can keep
paragraphs: Build the transfer package while operating, not after receiving an offer. Under 17 U.S.C. section 204(a), a copyright ownership transfer generally requires a writing signed by the owner or their authorized agent. Obtain signed assignments for custom scripts, copy, documentation, and other transferable work; identify excluded pre-existing materials and the licenses needed to use them. Do not assume contractor payment creates ownership or that every commissioned asset qualifies as work made for hire. Separately inventory domains, telephone numbers, trademarks without decorative symbols, CRM configurations, customer contracts, and licensed data. A copyright assignment does not override data-provider restrictions, privacy duties, or a customer's contractual limits. Review assignment and change-of-control clauses before promising contract transferability. Use business-controlled administrative accounts with named individual access, recovery procedures, and audit logs; never make a buyer dependent on a departing contractor's personal mailbox. For customer and prospect records, document permitted uses, retention schedules, suppression obligations, and any transaction-related transfer conditions. For covered California businesses, evaluate sale, sharing, and service provider obligations under the California Consumer Privacy Act, including Civil Code sections 1798.100 and 1798.120. B2B contact information is not categorically outside that framework.

Price the business using a clearly named earnings measure rather than multiplying revenue because the service uses automation. For illustration only, evaluate a small owner-operated book at two to three times normalized seller discretionary earnings, and a genuinely manager-run operation at three to four-and-a-half times normalized EBITDA. These are underwriting sensitivities, not observed transaction comparables or promised bids. Smaller, concentrated, project-heavy books can warrant less; verified retention, clean rights, and low founder dependence may support stronger pricing. Canonical owner net profit is not automatically either valuation denominator. If a reconciliation establishes that Base's $127,500 equals normalized seller discretionary earnings, the illustrative enterprise value range is $255,000 to $382,500. If that same profit excludes compensation for necessary owner work, an assumed $90,000 replacement cost leaves $37,500 before other normalization adjustments. Likewise, Scaled's $300,000 less an assumed $110,000 replacement cost leaves $190,000; if this reconciles to normalized EBITDA, the illustrative range becomes $570,000 to $855,000. Deduct replacement cost only once and only when it is absent from recorded expenses. Neither exercise changes the canonical scenario profits or establishes a market clearing price.

Separate headline enterprise value from cash delivered to the seller. In an illustrative $700,000 transaction, twenty percent contingent consideration leaves $560,000 payable before closing adjustments; debt repayment, working-capital adjustments, fees, taxes, and any escrow further change immediate proceeds. Specify whether an earnout measures retained collected revenue, gross contribution, or another auditable outcome, and define customer attribution and buyer operating obligations. A vague earnout can transfer pricing and staffing risk back to the seller after control has changed. Assemble twenty-four months of monthly statements when available, with younger books showing their complete operating history rather than fabricated longevity. Include cohort exports, customer concentration, rights assignments, contractor agreements, incident history, and a reconciliation from reported profit to the proposed earnings denominator. Test a two-week founder absence at Scaled, measuring service attainment, accepted outcomes, collections, and renewal progress. If the operation fails that test, improve delegation before claiming manager-run economics. For a durable cash cow, use the same controls but distribute only cash remaining after taxes, reserves, and working-capital needs. Candidate #18's 54 mapped plays create value through repeatable ownership and evidence, not through the size of the documentation folder.

chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #18, Commercial Lead Generation, holds Rank #05 with an 89/100 Money-to-Manpower Score and 54 mapped plays. This sprint turns that opportunity into a four-person operating system: one full-time owner plus three contractors cover targeting, inbox operations, and qualification. Days 1–7 establish the offer and evidence controls; Days 8–14 test outreach; Days 15–21 validate appointments and client acceptance; Days 22–30 reconcile cash and select Kill, Fix, or Scale. The canonical annual owner-profit cases are $20,000 Conservative, $127,500 Base, and $300,000 Scaled, excluding client-funded advertising pass-through from operator revenue. A $5,000 first-month cash-burn ceiling, explicit sample requirements, and separate acquisition and delivery scoreboards prevent early activity from masquerading as a repeatable business.

sections.heading: 1. Days 1–7: Bound the Offer, Assign the Pod, and Instrument Every Handoff
paragraphs: Start with one commercial buyer, one territory, and one acceptance definition, rather than launching a general appointment agency. A workable initial segment is regional commercial HVAC contractors selling maintenance agreements to facilities managers at multi-site businesses. Define an accepted appointment as a held conversation with an eligible decision-maker, inside the contracted territory, with a documented service requirement and an agreed next step. A calendar booking alone earns no accepted-appointment fee. On Day 1, the owner writes the exclusions, duplicate lookback, dispute window, and replacement treatment into a two-page pilot scope. Candidate #18 has 54 mapped operator plays; use a proposed sprint allocation of 12 offer-and-control slots, 14 acquisition slots, 16 delivery slots, and 12 reporting-and-retention slots. These allocations organize the supplied total, rather than assert titles for an unavailable play inventory. Link each actual play identifier to a deliverable before declaring coverage. Keep all 54 visible, but activate only the dependencies needed for the first pilot. The owner alone changes pricing and acceptance rules, preventing contractors from quietly selling different promises to different prospects during the same measurement cohort.

Assign the four-person pod by failure domain. The full-time owner handles discovery, proposals, client acceptance disputes, and cash. The research contractor owns account selection and source provenance; the infrastructure contractor owns Google Workspace configuration, HubSpot fields, and suppression synchronization; the qualification contractor owns callbacks, appointment evidence, and disposition coding. Contractors receive bounded assignments, not an assumption of full-time availability. For the initial month, reserve 30 research hours at $25, 20 infrastructure hours at $40, and 30 qualification hours at $25, totaling $2,300. Reserve $650 for inboxes, domains, CRM, and scheduling; $450 for data and verification; $300 for telephone routing; $300 for targeted professional review; and $1,000 contingency. The resulting $5,000 cash ceiling excludes owner living costs and contains no client advertising advance. Set cumulative spending limits of $1,500, $2,750, $3,875, and $5,000 at Days 7, 14, 21, and 30. Record owner hours separately so apparently inexpensive delivery cannot conceal an overloaded founder. Release contingency only against a named defect, written estimate, and measurable completion criterion; buying another database is not a repair plan by itself.

Build the evidence model before importing contacts. HubSpot needs account ID, contact source, collection date, geography, campaign cohort, suppression status, permission evidence where required, appointment outcome, client disposition, and fee eligibility. Google Workspace sender domains need correctly published SPF and DKIM records plus DMARC reporting and alignment checks. Use clearly identified business domains, never misleading lookalikes. Separate agency-acquisition records from client-delivery records because their denominators answer different questions. An agency sales meeting cannot become a delivered client lead. Commercial email under 15 U.S.C. § 7704 requires accurate routing information, nondeceptive subjects, applicable identification, a valid postal address, and a working opt-out; process opt-outs immediately operationally, within the statutory outside deadline. Telephone review must address 47 U.S.C. § 227, 47 CFR § 64.1200, and applicable state restrictions based on destination, technology, and message purpose. A business title does not establish that a number is a business landline. Configure Twilio initially for inbound routing and permitted manual callbacks, with recording disabled until applicable notice and permission requirements are resolved. Run synthetic records through every route before a real prospect enters the system.

sections.heading: 2. Days 8–14: Test Acquisition Without Mistaking Inbox Activity for Demand
paragraphs: Use Days 8–14 to test whether the selected buyer recognizes the problem and will discuss a paid pilot. Prepare 150 verified agency-acquisition contacts, divided into two 75-contact cells with comparable account size and territory. These are prospects for the agency, not leads delivered to a client. Change only the offer framing between cells: maintenance-pipeline visibility versus qualified facilities conversations, for example. Keep sender identity, contact selection, timing, and follow-up rules otherwise stable. Begin with a small manually reviewed batch and increase only after authentication, reply handling, and suppression work correctly. Multiple inboxes provide legitimate ownership and continuity; they do not justify multiplying volume to escape provider limits. Follow provider terms and stop rather than rotate domains after enforcement. Avoid artificial warm-up networks and engagement exchanges. Each message should reference a verifiable commercial circumstance, not invented familiarity or fabricated customer results. End the week with actual conversations, recorded objections, and a corrected offer. A weak first cell is a research result, not permission to purchase thousands of similar addresses before understanding why the selected buyers ignored it.

Define measurement rules before comparing variants. Unique delivered contacts equal attempted unique contacts minus hard bounces; count a person once per cohort despite follow-ups. Positive replies express relevant interest or request a substantive commercial discussion; automated replies, referrals without engagement, and polite refusals do not qualify. Mature each contact for seven calendar days after first delivery before using reply results in a checkpoint. Report booked, held, and qualified-held meetings separately. A qualified-held agency meeting requires the buyer profile, a relevant demand problem, and a concrete next step. For client delivery, maintain a separate accepted-submission rate and held-to-booked rate, with exclusions fixed in advance. Investigate any spam complaint immediately and pause the affected source or message while investigating; provider enforcement requires an immediate stop. Pause a source when hard bounces exceed 2% across at least 100 attempts, or when three hard bounces appear in any smaller launch batch. These are internal risk controls, not provider safe harbors. Do not optimize open rates: image blocking and automated fetching make them poor evidence of buyer demand or message quality.

Make the paid pilot commercially simple enough to sell and operationally narrow enough to fulfill. An illustrative offer is a $1,500 service retainer for a defined pilot period plus $100 for each accepted held appointment, with an initial cap of ten billable appointments. Specify what the retainer buys, how duplicate contacts are treated, and when disputed submissions must receive evidence-backed decisions. Cash collected upfront remains distinct from revenue earned as services are performed. Use Stripe or ACH invoices with clear service descriptions and keep the client's advertising account and funding separate. Never book the client's advertising spend, resulting sales, or contract value as agency fee revenue. During discovery, ask who can accept appointments, what calendar capacity exists, and how quickly the client will return dispositions. A client with no available salesperson can destroy a sound campaign through missed calls. Candidate #18's first-deal range is 1–4 months, so a Day 14 launch should produce tested mechanics and credible buying signals rather than an invented contract. If nobody buys, continue only within the approved test budget and repair a specific commercial hypothesis.

sections.heading: 3. Days 15–21: Prove Acceptance, Reconcile Unit Costs, and Remove Manual Breakpoints
paragraphs: Days 15–21 move from message testing to operational proof. If a pilot has sold, onboard exactly one client before replicating the workflow. Capture service territory, excluded accounts, incumbent relationships, buyer roles, calendar capacity, and the designated acceptance contact. Configure a client-specific HubSpot pipeline and routing destination without copying unrestricted access across accounts. Give contractors only the records required for their assignments. Submit each appointment with evidence of fit, the prospect's expressed requirement, meeting attendance, and the agreed next step. Require client disposition within three business days under the pilot agreement, but do not silently convert delayed responses into accepted fees. Escalate late decisions to the owner and exclude unresolved submissions from mature acceptance-rate calculations. Report their count and age separately so delays remain visible. If no client has bought, use clearly labeled synthetic delivery records to test mechanics and continue agency acquisition. Synthetic records never enter market-performance numerators. This branch preserves useful progress without manufacturing acceptance evidence, spending on speculative client campaigns, or making Day 21 revenue appear mandatory despite the stated first-deal time range.

Calculate delivery contribution using earned service revenue, not calendar activity or bank deposits alone. Suppose one completed pilot earns its $1,500 retainer and ten accepted-appointment fees of $100, producing $2,500 revenue. Direct contractor delivery costs of $900, attributable data and software of $250, and telephone charges of $100 leave $1,250 contribution, or 50%, before shared overhead and owner economics. A rejected appointment earns no acceptance fee; a replacement consumes capacity and its actual cost stays in the ledger. Allocate shared subscriptions once using a documented rule, avoiding double counting between acquisition and delivery. Track agency customer acquisition cost separately as acquisition spending divided by newly paying clients, while recording owner sales hours alongside it. With no paying clients, report spending and zero wins rather than a fabricated ratio. For a first client, divide acquisition cost by observed monthly contribution only when that contribution exists and is reasonably repeatable. A single pilot cannot establish lifetime value. This distinction prevents a high retainer deposit from disguising expensive fulfillment, repeated replacements, and an owner who must personally rescue every appointment.

Reconcile the operating model to the canonical scorecard before discussing expansion. Conservative revenue of $100,000 could comprise two $3,000 monthly retainers for twelve months, yielding $72,000, plus 280 accepted appointments at $100, yielding $28,000. The 20% net margin leaves $20,000 annual owner profit and $80,000 total modeled costs with 1 FT + 3 C. Base revenue of $425,000 could comprise five $5,000 monthly retainers, yielding $300,000, plus 1,250 accepted appointments at $100, yielding $125,000. At 30.0%, owner profit is $127,500 and modeled costs are $297,500 with the same pod. Scaled revenue of $750,000 could comprise ten $5,000 monthly retainers, yielding $600,000, plus 1,500 accepted appointments at $100, yielding $150,000. At 40%, owner profit is $300,000 and modeled costs are $450,000 with 2 FT + 4 C. These are illustrative fee compositions of exact annual targets, not first-month forecasts. Base delivery implies roughly 104 accepted appointments monthly across five clients; prove staffing capacity before selling that load. Different retainer scopes explain why appointment volume alone cannot predict total revenue or profit.

sections.heading: 4. Days 22–30 and Beyond: Apply Sample-Aware Kill, Fix, or Scale Decisions
paragraphs: Use the final nine days to close evidence gaps rather than maximize send counts. Day 22 audits targeting and suppression; Day 23 starts the last acquisition contacts eligible to mature by Day 30. Day 24 reviews proposals and objections; Day 25 reconciles client dispositions; Day 26 locks cost attribution; Day 27 reviews contractor capacity; Day 28 tests reporting recovery; Day 29 freezes the checkpoint packet; Day 30 records the decision. For agency acquisition, the cumulative mature sample floors are 300 unique delivered contacts at Day 30, 600 at Day 60, and 1,000 at Day 90. Require positive replies of at least 2% and qualified-held meetings of at least 1% at each checkpoint. The corresponding minimum counts are six and three, twelve and six, then twenty and ten. Preserve source and variant cuts because cumulative averages can hide deteriorating recent performance. Contacts still within seven days of first delivery remain pending. An underpowered cohort receives Fix or a bounded extension, not a declaration that the market has failed. Missing revenue at Day 30 alone does not justify killing an opportunity whose first deal can require four months.

Scale requires delivery proof as well as acquisition response. At Days 30, 60, and 90, require at least 10, 20, and 30 resolved client submissions respectively, acceptance of at least 80%, and held-to-booked performance of at least 70% across at least 10, 20, and 30 due bookings. Due bookings exclude future meetings; resolved submissions exclude pending client decisions. Require delivery contribution of at least 40%, 45%, and 50%, respectively, using actual earned revenue and attributable costs. Commercial proof rises from one paying pilot and $1,500 cumulative collected service fees, to one renewing or extending client and $3,000 collected, to two active paying clients and $6,000 collected. Collections exclude advertising funds and refundable security deposits. At Day 90, require the oldest eligible client to renew or extend; if no client has reached a decision date, retention remains unproven. Keep all acquisition, delivery, cash, and capacity conditions conjunctive: passing one does not offset failing another. Day 30 Scale therefore means a controlled next test, not an automatic staff expansion. Increase approved contact volume or client capacity by no more than 25% per two-week cycle, changing only one dimension.

Kill the affected channel immediately for a material permission failure, ignored opt-outs, or provider enforcement; preserve evidence and investigate before any restart. Stop discretionary spending when its ceiling is reached. For commercial viability, Day 60 Kill applies when two sequential repaired tests, each with at least 300 mature delivered contacts, produce zero positive replies. Day 90 Kill applies when two completed delivery repair cycles still leave contribution below 20% on at least 30 resolved submissions, or when at least ten qualified-held agency meetings and five written proposals produce zero collected service fees. These are internal stop rules for this offer and segment, not universal market verdicts. All other misses enter Fix with one owner, one hypothesis, and a fourteen-day deadline. Authorize no more than $2,500 additional gross cash spending per extension, without automatic renewal; cumulative ceilings become $10,000 at Day 60 and $15,000 at Day 90 if both monthly extensions are approved. Require committed cash for remaining obligations before authorizing each extension. Reserve 20% of pod capacity for defects and client response. Expand beyond 1 FT + 3 C only after measured workload supports the canonical Scaled configuration of 2 FT + 4 C.
